params.textField: Cholestyramine is considered a bile acid sequestrant. Bile, which is rich in cholesterol, is normally excreted from the liver into the canaliculi and off to the gall bladder, and then into the *small intestines*. But much of that bile is then *reabsorbed* and taken back into the *liver*. What cholestyramine does is to decrease the reabsorption of much of that cholesterol. But cholestyramine has its problems. Firstly, the liver often attempts to compensate for the decreased reabsorption of cholesterol by making more of the *LDL*, the bad cholesterol protein. Cholestyramine also tastes terrible and binds fat soluble vitamins, *A, D, K and E* and many *drugs*. The medication also causes *constipation*. So, it is not one of our preferred lipid-lowering drugs, but it does have its merits, as it can decrease some therapy-resistant *diarrhoea* including that caused by *Chron’s disease*. It is also useful in treatment of GIT *clostridium* infections as it binds the bacterial *toxins* and decreases the diarrhoea.

answers.text: Unlike most combinations of lipid lowering medications, ezetimibe can be combined with atorvastatin or other statins and that does not increase the risk of rhabdomyolysis
Fixed pill combinations of Ezetimibe and atorvastatin are available.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No, this statement is incorrect.  Ezetimibe only has the one action of decreasing absorption of cholesterol, and does not even decrease absorption of triglycerides. The statins have antithrombotic, antioxidant and plaque stabilizing effects and ezetimibe can be combined with one of those to achieve those actions.
